findings.source_quote: οὔτε ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων γενέσθαι τί οὐσίαν ἔχει δύναται
findings.english_quote: Nor can anything that has substance come into being out of what does not exist.
findings.issue: The English can be defended as a contextual unpacking of the compressed construction, but the note does not adequately explain that unpacking. The supplied reading contains finite ἔχει alongside δύναται, not a participle or an expressed relative pronoun. Calling τί οὐσίαν ἔχει the subject and glossing it as “anything that has substance” leaves the crucial syntactic linkage unexplained. A parenthetic understanding of οὐσίαν ἔχει, “it has substance,” is also possible and need not carry exactly the restrictive scope of the English relative clause. This is an interpretive disclosure problem; the confirmed print is not thereby an OCR error.
findings.suggested_revision: Expand the source-quoted note to explain the proposed loose or parenthetic predication and why the context supports expressing it attributively as “that has substance.” Preserve the alternative parenthetic linkage and its possible scope difference. Explicitly retain the supplied ἔχει; do not silently replace it with ἔχον or insert a Greek relative pronoun. The resulting wording and explanation require fresh review.

findings.source_quote: τοῦτο ὄντως εἶναι χαλεπὸν δικαίως τὸν κακῶς προδιωρισμένον ὀρθῶς ἔχειν εἰπόντος
findings.english_quote: this is indeed grievous, with the one who said that the previously badly defined [one] was right speaking justly.
findings.issue: A defensible grammatical analysis is available: εἰπόντος can form a genitive absolute with its speaker unexpressed, δικαίως qualifies the saying, and τὸν κακῶς προδιωρισμένον supplies the accusative subject of ὀρθῶς ἔχειν. The unidentified speaker and the alternative referents already disclosed in the note do not themselves establish source corruption or require a publication block. Nevertheless, “the one who said ... speaking justly” is unnecessarily difficult English: it distributes one participle across a relative clause and an additional participial phrase, making the relationship of the saying to “justly” hard to follow. This finding concerns intelligibility, not a demonstrated missing Greek clause.
findings.suggested_revision: Consider the more transparent formulation “this is indeed grievous, with someone justly saying that the previously wrongly defined [one] is correct.” Explain the implied-subject genitive-absolute analysis in the note, retain the person/being versus understood λόγον alternatives, and leave the referents unidentified. Reassess the note’s blocking classification on that grammatical basis rather than merely because a literal rendering exists. This proposed formulation has not itself been accepted and requires fresh review.

findings.source_quote: ὅθεν ἀθανασίας ἐπικρατούσης εὐλόγως πάντα γεγονότα φανήσεται.
findings.english_quote: Hence, when immortality prevails, it will become apparent that everything has come into being with good reason.
findings.issue: The draft attaches εὐλόγως to the coming into being expressed by γεγονότα, producing a claim about the rationale of everything’s origin. That is defensible in the surrounding discussion of the usefulness and suitability of created things. However, εὐλόγως can instead qualify φανήσεται, expressing the reasonableness of the appearance or inference. This material attachment alternative is not disclosed in the notes.
findings.suggested_revision: Add a source-quoted note explaining that the main text reads εὐλόγως with γεγονότα, “has come into being with good reason,” because the surrounding argument discusses the purposes of things. Preserve the alternative attachment to φανήσεται, approximately “it will reasonably appear that everything has come into being.” Do not present either attachment as uniquely established. Submit the amended passage and note for fresh review.
